name: Jamal Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a jumbo at an underground zinc and lead mine. A jumbo is a drill rig with two long arms; I drill the rock face at the end of a new tunnel, about forty-five holes, so the charge-up crew can load explosives and blast another four metres. Then we bolt and mesh the roof so it's safe, and do it all again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it takes skill to read the rock: you feel a soft patch through the controls before you see it. What wears me out is the heat at the bottom levels and the water dripping on you all shift. And driving forty minutes home at seven in the morning after nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with the job. At work nobody talks about AI much anyway; we talk about the ground and the bonus. If my cousin posted something about it in the family chat, I'd send a thumbs up and leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life goes the way I planned. Zinc's steady, the mine has twelve years of ore in the plan, and a good jumbo operator always has work. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and keep sending my mum 400 a month, like I have since Dad died. Hana and I would keep saving for the wedding in 2028; we've got about three months of costs put away. And I'd sit my shotfirer's licence next year, the licence to handle and fire explosives, because that's the next step up underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I already know, and I know how to do well in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a normal weekend look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We drive up to my grandfather's place most Sundays, after church. He's got a vegetable patch and a bad hip, so I do the digging and he tells me I'm doing it wrong. That's my week, really: the mine, Hana, Mum and the old man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about money or work that does keep you up at night, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. The rent's fine, the job's steady, and nobody at our mine has been laid off in the four years I've been there. If anything, it's the heat and the hours that might push me to change, not AI.

say: I'd say **good, let's get on** with the job.
At work people talk about the ground and **the bonus**, not AI, and online he'd just send a thumbs up.
think: His life goes **as planned**, with twelve years of ore in the mine plan.
A good **jumbo operator** always has work, so he feels secure.
do: Keep drilling and keep sending his mother **400 a month**.
Keep saving with Hana for their **2028 wedding** on top of three months' savings.
Sit his **shotfirer's licence** next year as the next step underground.
feel: **Calm**, because it's the world he knows and knows how to do well in.
S0.quote: Zinc's steady, the mine has twelve years of ore in the plan, and a good jumbo operator always has work.
fieldNote: He supports his **widowed mother** every month, which shapes every money decision.
Weekends revolve around **church and his grandfather**, a picture of steady family duty.
His only real strain is **heat and hours**, not job security.

steps.text: Keep drilling development headings on the jumbo
Keep saving with Hana for the 2028 wedding
Sit the shotfirer's licence for handling explosives next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the mine's not an office, so we'll feel it last. The planning and the paperwork, sure, let the computer do that. But I'd tell people underground that a drill still needs someone who can read the rock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the jumbos already have a mode where they drill the pattern by themselves while you watch. Nobody uses it much yet because our ground's broken and wet and it keeps stopping. If robots spread slowly, I've got years, but I'd see it creeping in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go for the shotfirer's licence, and I'd learn the automatic drilling mode properly instead of switching it off like the rest of the crew. If the company runs a course on the new planning software, I'd do it once a couple of the others have tried it. I'd keep the savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Not scared, but I'd notice every time the bosses said "efficiency" at a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think gets it wrong in this kind of change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head office, the people who've never been down a decline in their lives. They make the plan on a screen in the city and we find out it's wrong at the face. If AI makes the plans, it'll be the same problem with fewer people to blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hana about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana would worry more than me; she's like that. I'd tell her the mine needs us for a long while yet, and that I'm getting my tickets so I'm not easy to replace. Her mother would probably tell her to marry a teacher.

say: He'd say the mine **isn't an office**, so it will feel change last.
He'd tell the crew a drill still needs someone who can **read the rock**.
think: The jumbos already have an **automatic drilling mode** that stops often in broken, wet ground.
With slow robots he has **years**, but he'd see automation creeping in.
do: Learn the **automatic drilling mode** properly instead of switching it off.
Take the **planning software** course once a couple of colleagues have tried it.
feel: A little **uneasy**, noticing every time bosses say "efficiency" at meetings.
S1.quote: If AI makes the plans, it'll be the same problem with fewer people to blame.
fieldNote: He blames **head office** planners who never go underground, not the technology itself.
He's **steady**: he'd learn new tools after a couple of colleagues go first.
His partner Hana is the **worrier**; he reassures her with his licences.

steps.text: Keep drilling on his usual roster underground
Sit the shotfirer's licence for handling explosives
Learn the jumbo's automatic drilling mode properly
Take the planning software course after colleagues try it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot, too fast, and the companies should be made to train their own people, not just buy machines. I'd say that to the shift boss and I'd say it after church. I wouldn't be shouting about handouts, though; I'd want work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the planning office and the engineers go first, in 2028. My job is hands-on, so I'd guess I've got until about 2031, maybe a bit longer underground because the ground's so rough. But three years goes fast when your mum's relying on 400 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get my shotfirer's licence and my ground-support ticket, so I can do the jobs around the drill, not just the drill. I'd push our savings from three months to six by cutting the car upgrade and eating out. And Hana and I would bring the wedding forward to next year, smaller, while I've still got steady pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. I'm not panicking, but it's the feeling when you hear the rock above you crack and you wait for the next sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the wedding forward instead of putting it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to be married to her, and I want it done properly while we can afford it. If it all goes bad in 2031, I'd rather face it as a husband than a fiancé. My grandfather married on a miner's wage in a bad year; we'll manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the family would you have to let down first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum first; she'd still get her money, even if it's less. Then Hana and the wedding. My cousins would have to understand that the extras, the birthday money, the help with their cars, would stop for a while.

say: He'd say companies should **train their own people**, not just buy machines.
He'd say it to the shift boss and after church, asking for **work, not handouts**.
think: Hands-on drilling gives him until **about 2031**, maybe longer in rough ground.
Three years goes fast with his **mother relying** on 400 a month.
do: Get his **shotfirer's and ground-support** tickets in the first year.
Push savings from **three to six months** by skipping the car upgrade.
Bring the **wedding forward** to next year, smaller, while pay is steady.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, like hearing rock crack overhead and waiting.
S2.quote: If it all goes bad in 2031, I'd rather face it as a husband than a fiancé.
fieldNote: He responds to a short timeline by **marrying sooner**, not later, out of tradition and duty.
His priority order is clear: **mother first**, then Hana, then extended family.
He sees the **three-year robot gap** as a window for more underground licences.

steps.text: Get the shotfirer's and ground-support tickets this year
Skip the car upgrade and build savings to six months
Bring the wedding with Hana forward to next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop pretending. At the pub after shift I'd tell the younger lads to get every ticket they can now. And I'd say the government should back apprenticeships, not cheques.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years and three more for the robots puts me around 2034, maybe longer underground. I'd be 35 with a few tickets and maybe a supervisor's job by then. It's tight, but I'd have a fair chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the licences over the next two years, the shotfirer's and the ground-support. Then I'd go for an underground supervisor role, because someone has to sign off that a heading is safe, robot or not. Hana and I would have the wedding in 2028 like we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's the kind of worry that makes you work harder, not the kind that stops you sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Couldn't AI do the supervisor's job too, by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I think the law will still want a person to sign off underground safety for a long time. That's a guess; I'm not a lawyer. If I'm wrong, at least I'll have the experience to move into something else, like mine rescue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you start using the AI tools the mine brings in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably once a few of the other operators have used it and it doesn't crash every shift. I'm not first in line, but I'm not last either. If it's good, I'll use it.

say: He'd say five years is enough **if people stop pretending**.
He'd urge young workers to get tickets, and back **apprenticeships, not cheques**.

At 35 with tickets and maybe a **supervisor role**, he'd have a fair chance.
do: Get the **shotfirer's and ground-support** licences over two years.
Aim for an **underground supervisor** role signing off on safe headings.
Keep the **2028 wedding** with Hana as planned.
feel: **Uneasy but steady**, the kind of worry that makes him work harder.
S3.quote: Someone has to sign off that a heading is safe, robot or not.
fieldNote: He bets the **law** will keep a human signing off underground safety, and admits it's a guess.
His fallback idea is **mine rescue**, staying close to the work he knows.
He'd adopt AI tools **mid-pack**, once others prove they work.

steps.text: Get shotfirer's and ground-support licences over two years
Apply for an underground supervisor role signing off headings
Keep the 2028 wedding with Hana as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so anyone who's caught out has only themselves to blame. Maybe that's harsh, but that's how I was raised. I'd still help anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, robots underground around 2039 means I'd be 40 with nearly twenty years in. I'd have the tickets, maybe a supervisor's job, maybe a house. I'd be more worried about my knees than about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as planned: licences in the next couple of years, the wedding in 2028, and a house deposit after that. I'd use the AI tools when the mine rolls them out properly. Around 2033 I'd sit down with Hana and look again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, because it's still the end of underground mining as I know it. But mostly fine; it's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had a son in that world, what would you tell him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son to learn a trade first and a screen second. My dad told me the same thing, without the screen part. Work with your hands, then you can always fall back on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean to you, if the job you know just ends around 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad used to say a man's job is to leave things better for his kids than he found them. If the mine goes to robots, I'd want to have built something by then: a house, a family, a name in the town. That doesn't need a jumbo.

say: He'd say **ten years is plenty**, so anyone caught out is mostly to blame.
He admits that sounds **harsh**, and he'd still help anyone who asked.
think: Robots around **2039** come when he's 40 with nearly twenty years in.
By then his **knees** worry him more than AI.
do: Get his **licences** in the next couple of years.
Marry Hana in **2028** and save for a house deposit afterwards.
Sit down with Hana **around 2033** to look at plans again.
feel: A little **uneasy** at the end of underground mining as he knows it.
Mostly **fine**, because it's a long way off.
S4.quote: A man's job is to leave things better for his kids than he found them.
fieldNote: He judges people who are caught out after ten years, then **softens** it straight away.
His sense of worth rests on family and a **name in town**, not the jumbo itself.
He'd teach future children **trade first, screen second**, echoing his father.

steps.text: Keep drilling headings on the jumbo through the decade
Get shotfirer's and ground-support licences within two years
Marry Hana in 2028 and then save for a house

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have three years to get married, look after Mum and find what comes after the jumbo. What would help is apprenticeships for new trades that pay while you learn, and companies having to give miners first shot at the new jobs. Not a cheque in the mail; I'd want to earn it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the crew. Underground, you trust the people around you with your life every shift. If robots come, I don't just lose a job; I lose the people I'd trust in a fire.

headlineQuote: If robots come, I don't just lose a job; I lose the people I'd trust in a fire.
portrait: Jamal is 27 and runs a **jumbo drill** in an underground zinc and lead mine, drilling new tunnels.
He sends his widowed **mother 400 a month** and plans to marry his partner Hana in 2028.
He's traditional: he wants **work, not handouts**, and blames head office planners more than technology.
He's **steady** with change, adopting new tools once a couple of colleagues have proven them.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious** and pull the wedding forward; slower versions leave him uneasy but steady.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving three years to marry, support his mother and find work after the jumbo.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** in new trades while he learns.
